I've been working this land for 33 years. My father farmed before me. I know what grows here, what the soil needs, how deep the water table sits, and how many times I can run the pump before the electricity bill eats up the margin. My main rotation is wheat and maize — that's where my money comes from. The other crops fill in the edges and give the household food and some extra cash. My son works in the city now, so it's mainly me and my wife doing the field work, with some hired help at harvest.

Here's how I'll run things this year:

**Wheat and maize (15 mu):** This is my bread and butter. I use the same 15 mu for both, rotating. I'll plant wheat in October after maize harvest, rotary till the stalks under, use an improved variety — probably Jimai 22, same as last few years, good yield, decent disease resistance. I'll split fertilizer: base application before sowing, then topdress at jointing. Four irrigations: pre-sowing to get good germination, then jointing, heading, and grain filling. I've lost yield before skipping the heading watering. For maize I go hybrid — Zhengdan 958 or something similar from the village supply station. Strip sow right after wheat harvest in June, no-till to save time and moisture. Maize needs more nitrogen than wheat. I'll water at seedling establishment if it's dry, then at tasseling, then grain fill.

**Cotton (4 mu):** I've grown cotton here since I was young. Price has been unstable lately but I keep some because I know the crop well and the market usually comes back. I use Bt hybrid seed — cuts down on bollworm spraying, though I still need to spray for aphids and spider mites. Cotton needs more potassium than the grain crops. I'll plough this plot — cotton roots go deep and the soil needs loosening. More irrigations than cereals: budding, flowering, boll setting, and late boll period.

**Millet (1.5 mu):** Millet near the edge of the field where the soil is lighter and drier. It doesn't need much. I grow it for household use and to sell a little locally. One or two pump sessions if it doesn't rain in July. Traditional seed from my own stock. Light fertilizer.

**Mung bean (1 mu):** Legume, fixes nitrogen, gives the plot a break. We eat them at home and sell the rest. I don't push this crop hard — modest fertilizer, let it fix its own nitrogen, water once or twice. Rotary till before sowing.

**Peanut (1 mu):** I plough this plot deep because peanut pods grow underground and need loose soil. More potassium than the other crops. I'll water at flowering and pod fill. Improved seed from the co-op. The oil content is good with the local varieties they're selling now.
